title: Other Autoimmune Diseases: Systemic Sclerosis, Rheumatic Fever, and Sjogren Syndrome
subject: Immune System (IMMU)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers systemic sclerosis, acute rheumatic fever, Sjogren syndrome, neonatal lupus from maternal anti-Ro antibodies, and mixed connective tissue disease. Each is taught from mechanism to finding: how small vessel injury and TGF-beta driven fibrosis stiffen skin, gut, lung, and kidney; how antibodies raised against a streptococcal protein attack the heart; and how lymphocytes destroy exocrine glands. Board questions usually give an autoantibody, a preceding infection, or an organ pattern and ask you to name the disease, predict its complication, or explain its lesion. If you can link each antibody to its subset and explain why each complication follows, you can reason through most of these questions.
prerequisites: Hypersensitivity types I to IV and their effector mechanisms (IM-15-C)
Self-tolerance, its failure, and molecular mimicry (IM-13)
IgG structure and transplacental transfer through the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)
Group A streptococcus and its M protein (IM-14)
The renin-angiotensin system and the cardiac conduction system (CV-7)

connections.how: Rheumatic fever is the classic antibody-mediated (type II) example, while lupus shares anti-Ro antibodies and neonatal disease with Sjogren syndrome.
Chronic rheumatic heart disease remains a leading cause of mitral stenosis worldwide.
Maternal anti-Ro antibodies scar the fetal AV node and cause congenital complete heart block.

connections.how: Systemic sclerosis and mixed connective tissue disease cause interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, their main causes of death.

connections.how: Sjogren syndrome destroys salivary glands, and systemic sclerosis replaces esophageal smooth muscle with collagen.

terms.def: A chronic autoimmune disease of small vessel injury and excess collagen deposition in skin and internal organs; also called scleroderma.
Episodic cold- or stress-induced vasospasm of digital arteries producing white, then blue, then red fingers.
Thickened, tight skin of the fingers that limits their movement.
Abrupt severe hypertension and acute kidney injury from renal arteriolar narrowing and renin release in systemic sclerosis.
Cross-reaction of antibodies or T cells raised against a microbial antigen with a structurally similar self antigen.
The focal inflammatory lesion of acute rheumatic carditis, with fibrinoid change, lymphocytes, and activated macrophages.
An activated macrophage in an Aschoff body whose chromatin condenses into a slender wavy ribbon, giving the caterpillar cell appearance.
Clinical criteria that diagnose acute rheumatic fever from major and minor manifestations plus evidence of recent group A streptococcal infection.
Drying and injury of the cornea and conjunctiva caused by reduced tear production.
Autoantibodies against ribonucleoprotein antigens, typical of Sjogren syndrome and also found in lupus.
Disease of a fetus or newborn caused by maternal anti-Ro or anti-La IgG that crossed the placenta.
Antibody against the U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein of the spliceosome; at high titer it marks mixed connective tissue disease.

sections.title: Systemic sclerosis: vascular injury, autoimmunity, and fibrosis

blocks.text: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is a chronic autoimmune disease in which small blood vessels are injured and fibroblasts deposit excess collagen in the skin and internal organs. It affects women about three to four times as often as men and usually begins in middle age. Its cause is unknown, but three processes act together: microvascular injury, immune activation, and fibrosis.

Endothelial injury is the earliest change. Damaged endothelium releases endothelin, makes less nitric oxide, and allows platelets to adhere, so small arteries constrict and their intima proliferates until the lumen narrows. Capillaries are lost, which is visible as dilated and dropped-out nailfold capillaries. The tissue downstream becomes chronically ischemic. At the same time, CD4 T cells, many with a Th2 profile, infiltrate the skin and release IL-4, IL-13, and TGF-beta, and B cells make the autoantibodies that define the subsets (C02).

TGF-beta is the central fibrotic signal. Through SMAD signaling it converts fibroblasts into contractile myofibroblasts that produce type I and type III collagen and resist apoptosis, so collagen accumulates instead of being remodeled. Ischemia and repeated injury keep the fibroblasts activated. The result is the paired lesion of every affected organ: narrowed small arteries and dense collagen.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of systemic sclerosis
steps: Unknown trigger in a genetically susceptible person
Endothelial injury: more endothelin, less nitric oxide
Intimal proliferation narrows arterioles; capillaries are lost
T cells release IL-4, IL-13, and TGF-beta; B cells make autoantibodies
TGF-beta turns fibroblasts into collagen-producing myofibroblasts
Ischemia plus fibrosis in skin, gut, lung, kidney, and heart
blocks.caption: Vascular injury and immune activation converge on TGF-beta driven fibrosis, and ischemia keeps the cycle going.

blocks.title: Organ findings explained by mechanism
rows: Vasospasm on top of fixed intimal narrowing
Raynaud phenomenon in about 95%, often first; fingertip ulcers and pitted scars
Edema, then dense dermal collagen with loss of appendages
Puffy fingers, then sclerodactyly, tight face, small mouth
Smooth muscle of lower two thirds atrophies and is replaced by collagen
Dysphagia, low LES pressure, reflux, Barrett esophagus, strictures
Restrictive pattern with low DLCO; pulmonary arterial hypertension
blocks.caption: Each organ shows the same two lesions, narrowed small vessels and excess collagen, so its symptoms follow from lost blood flow or lost elasticity.

blocks.text: Raynaud phenomenon reflects this structure. Cold or stress constricts digital arteries whose lumens are already narrowed, so the fingers blanch white (ischemia), turn blue (deoxygenated blood pools), then flush red as flow returns (reactive hyperemia). The esophagus shows why fibrosis is so damaging: only its upper third is skeletal muscle, so the smooth muscle below fails, peristalsis disappears, and the weak lower esophageal sphincter lets acid reflux freely. Manometry therefore shows low LES pressure with absent distal peristalsis, the opposite of achalasia, where LES pressure is high and fails to relax. In the lung, interstitial collagen stiffens the parenchyma and thickens the alveolar wall, lowering lung volumes and diffusing capacity; lung disease is now the leading cause of death in systemic sclerosis.

blocks.predict: Two patients have dysphagia for solids and liquids. One has a low lower esophageal sphincter pressure with absent distal peristalsis; the other has a high LES pressure that fails to relax. Which has systemic sclerosis?
blocks.explain: The first. Collagen replaces the smooth muscle of the lower esophagus and sphincter, so the sphincter is weak and peristalsis is lost, causing reflux. Achalasia comes from loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons, so the sphincter stays tight.
blocks.check: The esophagus row of the organ table and the paragraph after it.

blocks.text: Systemic sclerosis is divided by how far skin thickening spreads, and the two subsets differ in antibody, pace, and the organ most likely to kill. Diffuse cutaneous disease involves skin proximal to the elbows and knees, including the trunk, and progresses quickly, with visceral fibrosis in the first few years. Limited cutaneous disease keeps skin changes distal to the elbows and knees and on the face, follows years of Raynaud phenomenon, and progresses slowly. Each subset has a characteristic antibody, and the antibodies are nearly mutually exclusive, so the antibody predicts the course.

blocks.title: Diffuse and limited systemic sclerosis compared
rows: Proximal limbs and trunk as well as hands and face
Interstitial lung disease, early and severe
Calcinosis, telangiectasia; association with primary biliary cholangitis
blocks.caption: Anti-Scl-70 points to diffuse skin disease and lung fibrosis; anticentromere points to CREST and late pulmonary hypertension.

blocks.text: CREST names the features of limited disease: calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. Calcinosis is dystrophic calcification, calcium salts deposited in damaged subcutaneous tissue of the fingers while serum calcium and phosphate stay normal. Telangiectasias are dilated capillaries and venules on the face, lips, hands, and gut mucosa, a sign of abnormal vascular repair, and gastrointestinal lesions can bleed. In limited disease the slow obliteration of small pulmonary arteries raises pulmonary vascular resistance, so pulmonary arterial hypertension and right heart failure appear many years after onset. Anticentromere antibodies give a distinctive discrete speckled pattern (centromere) pattern on immunofluorescence ANA testing.

Scleroderma renal crisis is the classic emergency of diffuse disease, especially early disease with rapidly spreading skin and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies. Intimal proliferation narrows the interlobular arteries in an onion-skin pattern, renal perfusion falls, and the juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Angiotensin II then raises blood pressure and constricts the already narrowed arterioles further, so ischemia and renin release reinforce each other. The patient develops abrupt severe hypertension, a rising creatinine, and often microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes as red cells shear on injured vessels.

blocks.title: Scleroderma renal crisis
steps: Endothelial injury narrows interlobular arteries and afferent arterioles
Juxtaglomerular cells sense low perfusion and release renin
Angiotensin II causes severe systemic hypertension
Angiotensin II constricts renal arterioles further
Renal perfusion falls more, releasing more renin
blocks.caption: A positive feedback loop: ischemia drives renin, and renin's product deepens the ischemia, causing acute kidney injury.

sections.title: Acute rheumatic fever: molecular mimicry and pancarditis

blocks.text: Acute rheumatic fever is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease that follows pharyngitis with group A streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) by about 2 to 4 weeks. It mainly affects children aged about 5 to 15 years and follows untreated or inadequately treated throat infection, often mild enough to go unnoticed; streptococcal skin infection can cause poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis but is not the classic trigger. The throat infection has often cleared by the time symptoms begin, because the disease is caused by the immune response, not by infection of the heart, so cultures of heart tissue and blood are sterile.

M protein is the main surface virulence factor of group A streptococcus; it resists phagocytosis, and antibody against it is protective. Some M protein epitopes resemble self proteins, especially cardiac myosin, tropomyosin, and laminin and other proteins of valve tissue. In a genetically susceptible host, antibodies and CD4 T cells raised against the bacterium cross-react with these self antigens, a process called molecular mimicry. Antibody binding to valve endothelium increases adhesion molecules so cross-reactive T cells enter the valve. Because antibody against a fixed tissue antigen starts the injury, rheumatic fever is classified as type II hypersensitivity, although T cells contribute heavily. The 2 to 4 week delay is the time needed to make these antibodies and expand the T cells.

blocks.title: From pharyngitis to rheumatic carditis
steps: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis, untreated
B and T cells respond to M protein
After 2 to 4 weeks, cross-reaction with cardiac myosin and valve proteins
Antibody activates valve endothelium; T cells enter
Pancarditis with Aschoff bodies; joints, skin, and brain also affected
blocks.caption: Molecular mimicry explains both the delay and the sterile inflammation.

blocks.text: The heart lesion is a pancarditis that inflames all three layers. The characteristic focus is the Aschoff body, which contains fibrinoid change of collagen, T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells. These have abundant cytoplasm and a central nucleus whose chromatin condenses into a slender wavy ribbon (caterpillar cells); some fuse into multinucleated Aschoff giant cells. Aschoff bodies heal into fibrous scars.

blocks.title: Pancarditis by layer
rows: Friction rub; usually resolves without sequelae
Aschoff bodies in interstitial connective tissue
Dilation, functional mitral regurgitation, heart failure; main cause of death in the acute phase
Valvulitis with fibrinoid necrosis and small (1 to 2 mm) verrucae along the lines of closure; MacCallum plaques in the left atrium
New regurgitant murmur; leaflet scarring that leads to chronic disease
blocks.caption: Only the valve injury commonly leaves permanent damage, which is why rheumatic fever is remembered for its valve disease.

blocks.predict: A child develops tea-colored urine 10 days after impetigo. Could this child develop rheumatic carditis from the same infection, and why are the two diseases classified differently?
blocks.explain: Classically no. Skin infection can cause poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis but is not the usual trigger for rheumatic fever, which follows pharyngitis. Glomerulonephritis is type III, from immune complexes deposited in glomeruli; rheumatic fever is type II, from antibody and T cell cross-reaction with cardiac antigens.
blocks.check: The first two paragraphs of this section and the type II and type III comparison in IM-15-C.

sections.title: Jones criteria and chronic rheumatic heart disease

blocks.text: Because no single test proves acute rheumatic fever, it is diagnosed with the Jones criteria (revised by the American Heart Association in 2015). A first episode requires evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection plus either two major manifestations or one major and two minor manifestations. Evidence of infection is a raised or rising antistreptolysin O (ASO) or anti-DNase B titer, a positive throat culture, or a positive rapid antigen test. Each major manifestation reflects mimicry in a different tissue.

blocks.title: Jones major manifestations
rows: New regurgitant murmur (usually mitral), rub, heart failure, or valvulitis seen only on echocardiography
Pancarditis; the only manifestation that can leave lasting damage
Migratory polyarthritis of large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists), very painful
Transient synovitis; an old clinical saying holds that rheumatic fever licks the joints but bites the heart
Rapid, purposeless movements, emotional lability; may begin months after infection
Antibodies cross-react with basal ganglia neurons
Evanescent, nonpruritic pink rings with clear centers on trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the face
Uncommon; lesions fade within hours and reappear, so they are easily missed
Painless firm nodules over bony prominences and extensor tendons
Central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by macrophages; usually seen with carditis
blocks.caption: Joints, skin, and brain recover; the heart is the organ that scars.

blocks.title: Jones minor manifestations (low-risk populations)
rows: Joint pain without objective arthritis (not counted if arthritis is a major criterion)
38.5 degrees C (101.3 degrees F) or higher
ESR 60 mm/h or higher, or CRP 3.0 mg/dL or higher
Adjusted for age (not counted if carditis is a major criterion)
blocks.caption: In moderate- and high-risk populations the 2015 revision lowers the thresholds and also accepts monoarthritis or polyarthralgia as major arthritis.

blocks.text: A prolonged PR interval reflects inflammation near the AV node and is a minor criterion, but it is not carditis. Chorea is the exception to the timing rule: it can appear months after infection, when antibody titers have fallen, and may then support the diagnosis on its own.

Chronic rheumatic heart disease develops after repeated or severe attacks. Valves heal by fibrosis and neovascularization: leaflets thicken, commissures fuse, and chordae tendineae shorten, thicken, and fuse. The mitral valve is affected in nearly all cases, alone or with the aortic valve, because the left-sided valves close against the highest pressures. Fused commissures produce a narrow fish-mouth orifice, so chronic rheumatic disease is the leading cause of mitral stenosis. Flow across the narrow valve needs a higher left atrial pressure, which enlarges the atrium, predisposes to atrial fibrillation and mural thrombus, and raises pulmonary venous and then arterial pressure. Scarred valves also attract infective endocarditis.

blocks.title: Applying the Jones criteria
blocks.text: A 9-year-old has had swollen, painful joints for 10 days: first the left knee, then the right ankle, then the left wrist. Temperature is 38.9 degrees C (102.0 degrees F), ESR is 75 mm/h, and there is a new apical holosystolic murmur. Three weeks ago she had a sore throat that was never treated. ASO titer is high. Migratory polyarthritis and carditis are two major criteria, and the high ASO gives evidence of infection, so the diagnosis is made. Fever and ESR are minor criteria and are not needed. The murmur is acute mitral regurgitation from valvulitis. If attacks recur, the valve will scar and decades later stenosis, not regurgitation, will dominate.

sections.title: Sjogren syndrome: autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands

blocks.text: Sjogren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease in which lymphocytes infiltrate and destroy the lacrimal and salivary glands, causing dry eyes and dry mouth. It affects women about nine times as often as men, usually in middle age. Primary Sjogren syndrome (sicca syndrome) occurs alone; secondary Sjogren syndrome accompanies another autoimmune disease, most often rheumatoid arthritis, and also lupus or systemic sclerosis.

Glandular epithelial cells appear to start and sustain the response. After an unknown trigger, possibly a viral infection, they express HLA class II and costimulatory molecules and release type I interferon and B cell activating factor (BAFF), so they present self antigen and keep lymphocytes alive. CD4 T cells gather around ducts, followed by B cells that can form germinal centers within the gland. Acinar and ductal cells are lost and replaced by lymphocytes and fibrosis, so tear and saliva secretion falls. Biopsy of minor labial salivary glands shows this focal periductal lymphocytic sialadenitis.

blocks.title: Manifestations explained by mechanism
rows: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca: gritty, burning eyes, corneal erosions
Lacrimal destruction lowers tear volume; low Schirmer test result
Xerostomia: dry mouth, trouble swallowing dry food, rampant dental caries, oral candidiasis
Less saliva to buffer acid, clear bacteria, and supply antimicrobial proteins
Extraglandular disease: arthralgia, interstitial lung disease, distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, peripheral neuropathy, palpable purpura
Lymphocytic infiltration of other epithelia and immune complex vasculitis
Anti-Ro (SSA), anti-La (SSB), ANA, rheumatoid factor, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia
blocks.caption: Gland loss explains the dryness; B cell hyperactivity explains the antibodies, the vasculitis, and the lymphoma risk.

blocks.text: Ro and La are intracellular ribonucleoproteins that become exposed on the surface of cells undergoing apoptosis, which may let them reach the immune system. Anti-Ro and anti-La are the characteristic antibodies, and rheumatoid factor is often positive even without arthritis. Anti-Ro is not specific: it also occurs in lupus, especially subacute cutaneous lupus, and it is the antibody that harms the fetus (C06).

The most serious complication is B cell lymphoma, mostly extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma arising in the salivary glands. Years of antigen-driven B cell proliferation inside the gland, supported by BAFF and rheumatoid factor producing clones, allow one clone to acquire mutations and grow independently of normal controls. Persistent parotid enlargement, purpura, low complement C4, cryoglobulins, or a new monoclonal protein signal this transformation. Dryness alone is not specific for Sjogren syndrome: anticholinergic drugs, radiation, aging, and infiltrative diseases also reduce secretion, so the antibodies or biopsy confirm it.

sections.title: Neonatal lupus and congenital heart block

blocks.text: Neonatal lupus is disease of a fetus or newborn caused by maternal anti-Ro (SSA) or anti-La (SSB) IgG. The mother may have Sjogren syndrome or lupus, but many mothers have no symptoms and learn of their antibodies only through the affected child. The infant does not have lupus; it is passively exposed to its mother's antibodies.

IgG is the only class that crosses the placenta. Syncytiotrophoblast cells take it up and protect it from degradation through the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), then release it into fetal blood. Transfer rises from the second trimester, the period when the fetal conduction system is developing. Anti-Ro antibodies bind Ro antigens exposed on fetal cardiomyocytes undergoing normal developmental apoptosis and may also interfere with L-type and T-type calcium channels, on which AV nodal conduction depends. Opsonized cells are taken up by macrophages, which release inflammatory and fibrotic signals including TGF-beta, so the AV node and surrounding tissue are inflamed, then fibrosed and calcified.

blocks.title: Congenital heart block from maternal anti-Ro
steps: Mother carries anti-Ro (SSA) IgG, with or without symptoms
FcRn carries IgG across the placenta in the second trimester
Antibody binds Ro exposed on fetal cardiac cells
Macrophage inflammation, then fibrosis and calcification of the AV node
Complete heart block with fetal bradycardia, usually from about 18 to 24 weeks
blocks.caption: The antibody is temporary, but the scar it causes is permanent.

blocks.text: Complete (third degree) heart block is the defining lesion. Atria are driven by the sinus node at a normal fetal rate while the ventricles follow a slow junctional or ventricular escape rhythm, so the fetal heart rate is persistently low with AV dissociation. Some fetuses also develop myocarditis, endocardial fibroelastosis, or dilated cardiomyopathy, which raise mortality. Only about 1 to 2% of pregnancies in anti-Ro positive women are affected, but the risk is much higher in a later pregnancy after one affected child, which shows that antibody is necessary but not sufficient.

blocks.title: Fixed versus transient findings of neonatal lupus
rows: Annular, photosensitive rash, often around the eyes
Depends on circulating maternal IgG, which is catabolized
blocks.caption: Damage that depends on continuing antibody resolves; damage that has already become scar does not.

blocks.predict: A newborn has a photosensitive rash around the eyes and a heart rate of 55 bpm with P waves unrelated to QRS complexes. The mother is well. Which findings will still be present at 1 year of age, and why?
blocks.explain: Only the complete heart block. Maternal anti-Ro IgG has a half-life of about 3 weeks and is gone within months, so the rash and any cytopenias resolve. The AV node was replaced by fibrous tissue before birth, and that scar remains.
blocks.check: The flow and the table of fixed and transient findings.

blocks.text: Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is an autoimmune syndrome that combines features of lupus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis in one patient, together with a high titer of antibody to U1 ribonucleoprotein (anti-U1 RNP). U1 RNP is part of the spliceosome, the complex that removes introns from pre-mRNA. Anti-Smith antibody, which is specific for lupus, binds the core Sm proteins shared by the same small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, so low titers of anti-U1 RNP are common in lupus. What defines MCTD is a high anti-U1 RNP titer without the antibodies that define the other diseases. The ANA is strongly positive with a speckled pattern.

blocks.title: Overlap features of mixed connective tissue disease
rows: Raynaud phenomenon (nearly all patients), puffy swollen hands, sclerodactyly, esophageal dysmotility, pulmonary hypertension
Diffuse truncal skin thickening, renal crisis
Severe lupus nephritis, CNS disease, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith
Proximal muscle weakness with raised creatine kinase
blocks.caption: MCTD usually spares the kidney and brain, the organs that make lupus most dangerous, but pulmonary arterial hypertension is its leading cause of death.

blocks.text: The mechanism follows the pattern of the parent diseases. Endothelial injury and intimal proliferation narrow digital and pulmonary arterioles, causing Raynaud phenomenon and pulmonary arterial hypertension; lymphocytic infiltration and immune complexes cause synovitis and serositis; and inflammatory infiltrates in muscle cause myositis. Puffy hands come from edema of the fingers, an early sign that may progress to sclerodactyly. Whether MCTD is a distinct disease or an early stage that later evolves into lupus or systemic sclerosis is debated, and some patients do evolve over years. On an exam, the combination of Raynaud phenomenon, swollen hands, myositis, and high-titer anti-U1 RNP without anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith points to MCTD.

blocks.title: Reading an autoantibody panel
blocks.text: A 34-year-old woman has Raynaud phenomenon, swollen fingers, proximal weakness with high creatine kinase, and arthritis. ANA is high titer, speckled. Step 1: anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are negative, so lupus is unlikely despite the arthritis. Step 2: anti-Scl-70 and anticentromere are negative, so diffuse or limited systemic sclerosis is unlikely despite the Raynaud phenomenon. Step 3: anti-U1 RNP is very high, which unites the three disease patterns as MCTD. Step 4: predict risk by mechanism. The kidney is usually spared, but the same arteriolar narrowing that causes her Raynaud phenomenon can obliterate pulmonary arterioles, so pulmonary arterial hypertension is the complication to anticipate.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology explain where these diseases strike. Systemic sclerosis injures the smallest arteries and the smooth muscle layers, so it damages the lower esophagus but spares its skeletal upper third, and narrowing of renal arterioles turns the juxtaglomerular renin response into a self-reinforcing crisis. Sjogren syndrome targets exocrine epithelium, so tear and saliva loss follow, while the fetal AV node is the only normal electrical path from atria to ventricles, so scarring it causes complete block. Placental physiology decides which antibodies matter: only IgG crosses, through FcRn, and it is cleared within months.

Microbiology, immunology, and pathology connect the triggers to the lesions. Rheumatic fever shows how a bacterial virulence factor can redirect immunity against the host through mimicry; systemic sclerosis shows how cytokines such as TGF-beta convert inflammation into fibrosis; and Sjogren syndrome shows how chronic antigen-driven B cell stimulation can end in lymphoma. In systemic sclerosis, Sjogren syndrome, and MCTD the autoantibodies mainly mark subset and prognosis, whereas in rheumatic fever and neonatal lupus antibody injures the target tissue directly. Their limits matter: anti-Ro and low-titer anti-U1 RNP also occur in lupus, and some patients have no subset antibody, so findings are interpreted together.

summary: Systemic sclerosis combines endothelial injury, T and B cell autoimmunity, and TGF-beta driven myofibroblast collagen deposition, producing narrowed small arteries and fibrosis in every affected organ.
Raynaud phenomenon, often the first sign, is vasospasm of already narrowed digital arteries; esophageal fibrosis gives absent distal peristalsis and a weak LES with reflux.
Interstitial lung disease (restrictive, low DLCO) and pulmonary arterial hypertension are the leading causes of death in systemic sclerosis.
Diffuse disease: proximal and truncal skin, anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I), early lung fibrosis, and renal crisis from a renin-angiotensin positive feedback loop.
Limited disease (CREST): distal skin, anticentromere, calcinosis with normal serum calcium, telangiectasia, and late pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Acute rheumatic fever follows untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis by 2 to 4 weeks; M protein mimicry of cardiac myosin and valve proteins (type II) causes pancarditis with Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells.

Jones criteria: evidence of streptococcal infection plus two major, or one major and two minor, manifestations; only carditis leaves lasting damage, and repeated attacks fuse mitral commissures into mitral stenosis.
Sjogren syndrome is lymphocytic destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands with anti-Ro and anti-La, often with RA, and a raised risk of marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma.
Maternal anti-Ro IgG crosses the placenta through FcRn and scars the fetal AV node, so congenital complete heart block is permanent while rash and cytopenias resolve.

Mixed connective tissue disease overlaps lupus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis with high-titer anti-U1 RNP, usually spares the kidney, and is most dangerous through pulmonary arterial hypertension.

verify: Jones criteria thresholds follow the 2015 American Heart Association revision for low-risk populations (fever 38.5 degrees C (101.3 degrees F), ESR 60 mm/h, CRP 3.0 mg/dL); confirm whether NABNE expects this revision or the older 1992 criteria.
Whether Sydenham chorea alone, without evidence of recent infection, suffices for diagnosis differs between older and revised Jones guidance; confirm the expected wording.

The statement that streptococcal skin infection does not cause rheumatic fever is the classic teaching, but some data from high-incidence populations suggest skin infection may contribute; confirm the NABNE position.
The latent period after pharyngitis is quoted as 1 to 5 weeks, 2 to 3 weeks, or 2 to 4 weeks in different sources; this chapter uses about 2 to 4 weeks.

Prevalence and ratio figures (female to male about 3 to 4:1 in systemic sclerosis and about 9:1 in Sjogren syndrome; Raynaud phenomenon in about 95% of systemic sclerosis; about 1 to 2% risk of congenital heart block in anti-Ro positive pregnancies; rash resolving by about 6 to 8 months) vary between sources and are given as approximate.
Classification of rheumatic fever as purely type II hypersensitivity is the board convention; Robbins emphasizes cross-reactive CD4 T cells as well.
Whether mixed connective tissue disease is a distinct entity or an early undifferentiated stage of lupus or systemic sclerosis remains debated; confirm how NABNE frames it.
